name: Babylonian Chronicle tablet BM 21946 (ABC 5)
findspot_description: Unprovenanced: purchased from a dealer in 1896; original excavation unknown.
description: Chronicle covering Nebuchadnezzar II's first eleven years: Carchemish (605), the accession, Levantine campaigns, and the capture of "the city of Judah" (597). Date of writing given as c. 595 BC by Wikipedia.

name: Jehoiachin's ration tablets (Babylon)
findspot_description: Vaulted building near the Ishtar Gate, Babylon (Koldewey excavations).
description: Oil ration lists naming Ya'u-kīnu, king of the land of Yahudu, and his sons among foreign recipients at the Babylonian court.

name: East India House Inscription
findspot_description: Ruins of Babylon; unearthed before 1803 by Sir Harford Jones Brydges.
description: Foundation inscription of Nebuchadnezzar II describing his temple building and devotion to the shrines of Babylon and Borsippa.

name: Cyrus Cylinder
findspot_description: Babylon, found by Hormuzd Rassam in March 1879; the article places it in the Esagila foundations, though Rassam gave conflicting locations.
description: Akkadian building inscription of Cyrus II proclaiming that Marduk let him enter Babylon without battle and denouncing Nabonidus.

name: Thiele (1983) divided-monarchy chronology
description: E. R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings, 3rd ed. Uses coregencies and differing regnal reckonings.

name: Albright (1945) divided-monarchy chronology
description: W. F. Albright, BASOR 100 (1945).

name: Septuagint (Greek) dates in Daniel
description: Dates found in Greek witnesses but absent from the Masoretic/Aramaic text. Kept separate so textual traditions are never mixed (SPEC 12.6).

name: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3 (Fall of Nineveh Chronicle)
Berossus, Babyloniaca (fragments)
description: History of Babylonia by the Babylonian priest Berossus, written in Greek c. 290–280 BC; survives only in quotations.

name: Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men (Greek additions to Daniel 3)
document_type: Deuterocanonical addition (non-canonical in the Protestant canon)
description: Prayer and hymn inserted after Dan 3:23 in Greek Daniel. Indexed as a textual source only (SPEC 5.6), not as Scripture of the 66-book canon.

name: Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242)
description: Fragmentary first-person account of Nabonidus afflicted for seven years at Tayma and healed by God, with a Judean urging public acknowledgement. Manuscript dated c. 75–25 BC; composition date disputed.

name: Nabonidus Cylinder from Ur
description: Foundation text for the ziggurat of Sin at Ur, found by J. G. Taylor in 1854 (four cylinders); ends with a prayer for Belshazzar, the eldest son. Museum numbers not verified.

name: Verse Account of Nabonidus
description: Hostile account of Nabonidus's reign: he entrusts the kingship to his eldest son, goes to Tayma, and is replaced by the pious Cyrus.

name: Behistun inscription of Darius I
document_type: Royal rock inscription (trilingual: Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian)
description: Darius I's account of his accession and the revolts of his first years, with a list of 23 subject lands (§6).

name: Kingdom of Judah
description: Southern Israelite kingdom with its capital at Jerusalem.

name: Kingdom of Israel (Northern Kingdom)
description: Northern Israelite kingdom with its capital at Samaria.

name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
description: Babylonian empire of the Chaldean dynasty, from Nabopolassar (626 BC) to the fall of Babylon (539 BC).

name: Egypt (Twenty-sixth Dynasty)
description: Saite dynasty of Egypt, including Necho II.

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
description: Persian empire founded by Cyrus II.

Governor of Gutium who entered Babylon with Cyrus's army "without a battle" on 16 Tašrītu and died on the night of 11 Arahsamna (ABC 7 iii 15–22). Often equated with the Gobryas of Xenophon.

Ruler who "received the kingdom" after Belshazzar's death, aged about 62 (Dan 5:31); "son of Ahasuerus, of the offspring of the Medes" (Dan 9:1). Not named in any known contemporary source; identification disputed (see the Daniel 5 dossier).
Median king, son of Astyages and uncle of Cyrus, in Xenophon's Cyropaedia (1.5.2). Not attested in Herodotus or cuneiform sources; his historicity is debated.
Achaemenid king (522–486 BC), author of the Behistun inscription; organised the satrapies and their tribute (Herodotus 3.89). Distinct from "Darius the Mede" of Daniel 5–6.

title: The four kingdoms and the everlasting kingdom (Dan 2:36–45)
speaker: Daniel
description: Daniel's interpretation: Nebuchadnezzar is the head of gold; three further kingdoms follow, the fourth strong as iron and later divided; in the days of those kings God sets up an everlasting kingdom that breaks the others.
in_text_interpretation: Only the first kingdom is identified in the text (Nebuchadnezzar / Babylon). The second, third and fourth kingdoms and the stone are not named in Daniel 2.

interpretations.label: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome; the stone is the messianic kingdom
proponents: Josephus (iron as a world-ruling power; declines to explain the stone)
Talmud and medieval Jewish commentators incl. Rashi
interpretations.summary: The metals are a historical succession ending with Rome; God's kingdom (the Messiah's) replaces the world empires. Josephus already reads the bronze as a power "from the west" and the iron as a dominion over all the earth.

interpretations.label: Rome with a future ten-kingdom phase; the stone is Christ's return
interpretations.summary: The fourth kingdom is Rome; the ten toes correspond to a future revived Roman confederation (cf. 7:24; Rev 17:12), not yet realised; the stone is the Messiah, whose return decisively ends the world kingdoms.

interpretations.label: Rome followed by the divided nations of Europe; the stone is God's unending kingdom at Christ's return
interpretations.summary: A continuous fulfilment through history from Babylon to Rome and its divided successors, culminating in God's kingdom.

interpretations.label: Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece (Seleucids and Ptolemies); the stone is God's imminent kingdom
proponents: Modern critical consensus, e.g. J. J. Collins (per Wikipedia)
Ephrem the Syrian; Polychronius; Cosmas Indicopleustes
interpretations.summary: Following Daniel's own sequence of Median and Persian rulers (5:31; 6:28), the four kingdoms are Babylon, Media, Persia and the Hellenistic kingdoms; the mixed iron and clay reflects Seleucid–Ptolemaic marriage alliances (c. 250 or 193 BC); the chapter in its present form dates from the early Seleucid period at the earliest.

referents.referent: God's kingdom expected to replace Hellenistic rule

title: The decree of the watchers against the king (Dan 4:19–27)
speaker: Daniel
description: Daniel interprets the tree as the king, who will be driven from human society to live like an animal for seven times until he acknowledges the Most High, after which his kingdom is restored; he urges repentance.
in_text_interpretation: The text identifies the tree as Nebuchadnezzar and narrates its fulfilment within the chapter (4:28–33).

interpretations.label: Fulfilled in Nebuchadnezzar's seven-year madness
interpretations.summary: The decree was fulfilled in the king's own humbling for seven years (as the Old Greek renders it) and his restoration.

interpretations.label: Originally about Nabonidus
interpretations.summary: The tale is a variant of a tradition about Nabonidus's affliction and his long stay at Tayma (cf. 4Q242), transferred to the better-known Nebuchadnezzar. This is a source-critical view, not a fulfillment claim.

title: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN (Dan 5:24–28)
speaker: Daniel
description: Writing on the palace wall which Daniel reads as: God has numbered the kingdom and ended it; the king is weighed and found wanting; the kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.
in_text_interpretation: Daniel's reading (5:26–28) and the narrated sequel that night (5:30–31).

interpretations.label: Fulfilled that night in the fall of Babylon
interpretations.summary: The kingdom of Belshazzar ended when Babylon passed to Cyrus in October 539 BC.

referents.referent: Babylon given to the Medes and Persians

interpretations.label: Weights and wordplay
interpretations.summary: As nouns the words name weights — a mina, a shekel and half-pieces — which Daniel reinterprets as verbs; parsîn also puns on "Persia". If the half-pieces are two half-shekels the total is 62 shekels, the age given for Darius the Mede. This is a reading of the words, not a fulfillment claim.

title: King of Babylon

start_window.basis: ABC 5: Nabopolassar died 8 Abu (15 Aug 605) and Nebuchadnezzar took the throne on 1 Ululu (7 Sep 605); Julian equivalents per Parker & Dubberstein as given by Livius.

end_window.basis: Last tablet of Nebuchadnezzar and first of Amel-Marduk dated to the same day, 7 Oct 562 BC (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, via Wikipedia); one-week window.

notes: Model-independent reconstruction from the Babylonian chronicles and the stated reign lengths; individual chronologists differ by months.
title: King of Judah

start_window.basis: Josiah was killed as Necho marched north (2 Kgs 23:29); the Egyptian army crossed the Euphrates against Harran in Du'ûzu 609 and besieged it until Ulûlu (ABC 3); Jehoahaz reigned three months (2 Kgs 23:31) before Necho installed Jehoiakim (2 Kgs 23:34). Conservative window 1 Aug 609 – 31 Jan 608.

end_window.basis: Jehoiachin reigned three months (2 Kgs 24:8; "three months and ten days", 2 Chr 36:9) before Jerusalem was taken on 2 Addaru of Nebuchadnezzar's 7th year (ABC 5), i.e. 15/16 March 597; Jehoiakim's reign therefore ended roughly Nov 598 – Mar 597.

notes: Babylonian accession-year dating; reign length 17 years (accession year 556/555).
title: King of Babylon

start_window.basis: Between Neriglissar's last text (12 Apr 556) and the end of June 556, by which Nabonidus was sole ruler; his first dated texts are from 25 May 556 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, p. 11).

end_window.basis: Babylon fell on 16 Tašrītu of year 17 (ABC 7 iii 15) = 13 Oct 539 in Parker & Dubberstein (1942, p. 11); other modern conversions give 12 Oct. A Nabonidus-dated tablet from Uruk of the next day reflects delayed news.

notes: Cyrus's reign as king of Persia began c. 559 BC; this record covers only his rule over Babylon, which the Babylonian documents date by.
title: King of Babylon and of the lands (Babylonian dating)

start_window.basis: Babylonian texts date Cyrus from the fall of Babylon, 16 Tašrītu (13 Oct 539 in Parker & Dubberstein; 12 Oct in other conversions); his accession year runs to Nisan 538, and year 1 begins 1 Nisan = 24 Mar 538.

end_window.basis: Last Cyrus-dated tablets 12 Aug 530; first Cambyses tablet as sole king 31 Aug 530 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, p. 12).

title: Carchemish: Nabopolassar year 21 (ABC 5) = Jehoiakim year 4 (Jer 46:2)
proposed_synchronization: Jeremiah 46:2 and the Babylonian Chronicle describe the same defeat of Necho II's army at Carchemish; the chronicle places it in Nabopolassar's 21st year, before his death on 8 Abu.
dating_method: Babylonian regnal year fixed to 605 BC by Ptolemy's Canon and astronomical texts (Parker & Dubberstein, via Livius)
assumptions: The Jeremiah superscription and the chronicle refer to one battle (both name Carchemish, Necho and Nebuchadnezzar).

window.basis: Narrated within Nabopolassar's 21st year (which began in Nisan 605, i.e. March/April) and before his death on 8 Abu = 15 Aug 605. Window starts 1 March for safety.

title: Capture of "the city of Judah" on 2 Addaru, Nebuchadnezzar year 7 (ABC 5) = Jehoiachin's surrender (2 Kgs 24:10–15)
proposed_synchronization: The chronicle's capture of the city of Judah and its king, and the installation of a king of Nebuchadnezzar's choice, correspond to Jehoiachin's surrender and Zedekiah's appointment.
dating_method: Babylonian date 2 Addaru, year 7 of Nebuchadnezzar = 15/16 March 597 BC (Parker & Dubberstein)
assumptions: "City of Judah" = Jerusalem; the unnamed king = Jehoiachin (identifications by the editors).
The 2 Kings event itself is to be researched in Milestone 6; this record documents the anchor used for Jehoiakim's reign end.

title: Jehoiakim year 4 = Nebuchadnezzar year 1 (Jer 25:1)
external_entity: Nebuchadnezzar II's regnal years (Babylonian, from ABC 5)
proposed_synchronization: Jeremiah 25:1 equates Jehoiakim's fourth year with Nebuchadnezzar's first; the Babylonian accession on 7 Sep 605 fixes Nebuchadnezzar's years.
dating_method: Nebuchadnezzar's accession year (Sep 605 – Nisan 604) and year 1 (Nisan 604 – Nisan 603)
assumptions: Whether Jeremiah counts Nebuchadnezzar's accession year as "first" is modelled as an alternative.

title: Fall of Babylon: 16 Tašrītu, Nabonidus year 17 (ABC 7)
proposed_synchronization: The Babylonian Chronicle dates the entry of Cyrus's army into Babylon to 16 Tašrītu of Nabonidus's 17th year; Daniel 5:28–31 places the end of Belshazzar's kingdom and its transfer to the Medes and Persians at that juncture.
dating_method: Babylonian day date converted with Parker & Dubberstein (1942) tables
assumptions: The chronicle year is lost on the tablet; the 17th year of Nabonidus is fixed by context and the Babylonian king-list chronology (Parker & Dubberstein).

window.basis: 16 Tašrītu year 17 = 13 Oct 539 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, p. 11; month VII began 28 Sep). Many modern works give 12 Oct; the one-day spread reflects day-boundary and month-start conventions. Window 12–13 Oct.

title: The great statue of four metals and the stone (Nebuchadnezzar's dream)

symbols.in_text_interpretation: Nebuchadnezzar: "You are the head of gold" (2:38).
Another kingdom, inferior, arising after Nebuchadnezzar (2:39); not named.
A third kingdom that will rule over all the earth (2:39); not named.
A fourth kingdom, strong as iron, that crushes all (2:40); not named.
A divided kingdom, partly strong and partly brittle; they will "mingle themselves with the seed of men" but not hold together (2:41–43).

symbols.description: Strikes the feet and becomes a great mountain
symbols.in_text_interpretation: A kingdom set up by the God of heaven "in the days of those kings", never to be destroyed (2:44–45).

description: A dream image: a great statue with head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, feet of iron mixed with clay; a stone cut out without hands strikes the feet, the statue is shattered, and the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth.

title: The great tree cut down (Nebuchadnezzar's second dream)

symbols.description: Reaches the sky, visible to the ends of the earth; shelter and food for all
A heavenly figure who decrees the felling
symbols.in_text_interpretation: The decree of the watchers / the Most High (4:17, 24).

symbols.symbol: Stump bound with iron and bronze
symbols.in_text_interpretation: The kingdom will be restored after he acknowledges Heaven's rule (4:26).

symbols.description: Period passing over the one with an animal's heart
symbols.in_text_interpretation: The king's period of exclusion until he knows that the Most High rules (4:25, 32).

description: A tree at the centre of the earth reaching to the sky, sheltering beasts and birds, is ordered cut down by a holy watcher; the stump is left bound with iron and bronze, and "seven times" pass over him.
